notes.front: What is a placard, in the Hazardous Materials Regulations?
notes.back: A hazard warning sign that subpart F requires on each side and each end of a bulk packaging, freight container, transport vehicle or rail car.
notes.explanation: Placards warn from outside the load: § 172.504(a) ties them to the containers and vehicles that carry hazardous material, not to the individual packages inside.
notes.example: Like the hazard label on a single drum, but for the outside of the whole truck, trailer, tank or rail car.
notes.evidence: each bulk packaging, freight container, unit load device, transport vehicle or rail car containing any quantity of a hazardous material must be placarded on each side and each end
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.504(a), PDF p. 284

notes.front: What is Table 1 in the placarding rules?
notes.back: The first placarding table in § 172.504(e). Its materials are placarded in any quantity, because the under-454 kg exception covers only Table 2.
notes.explanation: Paragraph (a) requires placards for any quantity, and the weight exception in paragraph (c) is written for Table 2 materials only, so no Table 1 material can use it.
notes.example: Like a list of items that always need a warning sign, however small the amount on board.
notes.evidence: Except for bulk packagings and hazardous materials subject to § 172.505, when hazardous materials covered by table 2 of this section are transported by highway or rail, placards are not required on
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.504(c) and (e), PDF p. 284

notes.front: What is Table 2 in the placarding rules?
notes.back: The second § 172.504(e) table. By highway or rail, under 454 kg of its materials in a vehicle or container needs no placards.
notes.explanation: The weight exception is the practical difference between the two tables; it does not reach bulk packagings or the materials in § 172.505.
notes.example: Like Table 1, but its materials get a weight allowance before placards are needed on the road or rail.
notes.evidence: A transport vehicle or freight container which contains less than 454 kg (1001 pounds) aggregate gross weight of hazardous materials covered by table 2 of paragraph (e) of this section
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.504(c)(1) and (e), PDF p. 284

notes.front: What is a subsidiary placard?
notes.back: A placard for a secondary (subsidiary) hazard, shown in addition to the placard for the material’s main hazard.
notes.explanation: § 172.505 requires some subsidiary placards and allows others: materials with secondary hazards may show them even when not required.
notes.example: Like a second warning sign on a tank of a flammable liquid that is also corrosive, beside its main one.
notes.evidence: Hazardous materials that possess secondary hazards may exhibit subsidiary placards that correspond to the placards described in this part, even when not required by this part
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.505(d), PDF p. 287

notes.front: What is the DANGEROUS placard?
notes.back: A placard that may replace separate Table 2 placards when non-bulk packages of two or more Table 2 categories share a vehicle or container.
notes.explanation: It saves displaying a separate placard for each Table 2 category in a mixed load of non-bulk packages. § 172.521 fixes its look: red upper and lower triangles.
notes.example: Like a single “mixed hazards” sign on a delivery van carrying small loads of several Table 2 classes.
notes.evidence: the DANGEROUS placard must have a red upper and lower triangle
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.504(b) and § 172.521, PDF p. 291

notes.front: Who must comply with the placarding requirements of subpart F?
notes.back: Each person who offers for transportation, or transports, a hazardous material subject to the regulations.
notes.explanation: Both the shipper and the carrier have placarding duties, which is why later sections split who provides and who affixes.
notes.evidence: Each person who offers for transportation or transports any hazardous material subject to this subchapter shall comply with the applicable placarding requirements of this subpart.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.500(a), PDF p. 283

notes.front: Does subpart F placarding apply to infectious substances?
notes.back: No. Subpart F does not apply to infectious substances.
notes.explanation: It is the first exclusion in § 172.500(b); Table 2 also lists Division 6.2 with no placard.
notes.evidence: This subpart does not apply to— (1) Infectious substances;
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.500(b)(1), PDF p. 283

notes.front: When is a limited quantity outside the placarding rules?
notes.back: When it is identified as a limited quantity on the shipping paper (§ 172.203(b)) or marked as one (§ 172.315).
notes.explanation: The exclusion depends on the material being declared or marked as a limited quantity, not just on its amount.
notes.evidence: Hazardous materials authorized by this subchapter to be offered for transportation as a limited quantity when identified as such on a shipping paper in accordance with § 172.203(b) or when marked as such in accordance with § 172.315.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.500(b)(2), PDF p. 283

notes.front: Are materials packaged as small quantities under §§ 173.4, 173.4a or 173.4b placarded?
notes.back: No. Subpart F does not apply to them.
notes.explanation: Those sections set their own packaging limits, and § 172.500(b)(4) takes such packages out of placarding.
notes.evidence: Hazardous materials which are packaged as small quantities under the provisions of §§ 173.4, 173.4a, 173.4b of this subchapter
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.500(b)(4), PDF p. 283

notes.front: Subpart F placarding does not apply to hazardous materials prepared in accordance with § {{c1::173.13}}.
notes.explanation: It is one of five exclusions in § 172.500(b), alongside infectious substances, limited quantities, small quantities and combustible liquids in non-bulk packagings.
notes.evidence: Hazardous materials prepared in accordance with § 173.13 of this subchapter;
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.500(b)(3), PDF p. 283

notes.front: A van carries 600 kg of a combustible liquid, all in non-bulk drums. Does subpart F require placards?
notes.back: No. Subpart F does not apply to combustible liquids in non-bulk packagings, whatever the weight.
notes.explanation: The exclusion is tied to the packaging: in a bulk packaging, a combustible liquid takes the COMBUSTIBLE placard from Table 2.
notes.evidence: (5) Combustible liquids in non-bulk packagings.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.500(b)(5), PDF p. 284

notes.front: Under § 172.502(a)(1), what three conditions must be met before anyone displays a placard?
notes.back: The material is a hazardous material; the placard represents a hazard of that material; and the placarding conforms to subpart F.
notes.explanation: All three must hold; § 172.502(b) lists the only exceptions to the prohibition.
notes.evidence: The material being offered or transported is a hazardous material; (ii) The placard represents a hazard of the hazardous material being offered or transported; and (iii) Any placarding conforms to the requirements of this subpart.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.502(a)(1), PDF p. 284

notes.front: What does § 172.502(a)(2) forbid besides wrong placards?
notes.back: Any sign, advertisement, slogan or device that, by colour, design, shape or content, could be confused with a placard.
notes.explanation: The rule gives “Drive Safely” as an example of a slogan that must not look like a placard.
notes.evidence: Any sign, advertisement, slogan (such as ‘‘Drive Safely’’), or device that, by its color, design, shape or content, could be confused with any placard prescribed in this subpart.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.502(a)(2), PDF p. 284

notes.front: Which markings does § 172.502(b)(2) except from the placarding prohibitions? Name two.
notes.back: Any two of: the BIOHAZARD marking; the “Hot” marking; the sour crude oil hazard marking; an identification number on a white square-on-point.
notes.explanation: These are markings the regulations themselves prescribe, so their display is not treated as prohibited placarding.
notes.evidence: The restrictions of paragraph (a) of this section do not apply to the display of a BIOHAZARD marking, a ‘‘HOT’’ marking, a sour crude oil hazard marking, or an identification number on a white square-on-point configuration
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.502(b)(2), PDF p. 284

notes.front: A van delivered Class 3 drums in the morning. In the afternoon it carries only non-hazardous goods, with the FLAMMABLE placards still on. Is that allowed?
notes.back: B: no. A placard may be displayed only when the material carried is a hazardous material whose hazard it represents.
notes.choices:
A) Yes, because permissive placarding allows placards at any time
B) No, a placard may not be displayed unless the load is a hazardous material with that hazard
C) Yes, if the placards are in good condition
D) Yes, until the end of the working day
notes.choicesExplained: A: permissive placarding in § 172.502(c) is for a hazardous material, when placards are not required. C: condition does not matter if the placard is prohibited. D: § 172.502 has no time allowance.
notes.explanation: Permissive placarding covers a hazardous material that does not need placards, not a load with no hazardous material at all.
notes.evidence: no person may affix or display on a packaging, freight container, unit load device, motor vehicle or rail car— (1) Any placard described in this subpart unless— (i) The material being offered or transported is a hazardous material;
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.502(a)(1), PDF p. 284

notes.front: May placards be displayed for a hazardous material when they are not required?
notes.back: Yes, if the placarding otherwise conforms to subpart F.
notes.explanation: This is permissive placarding; it still has to meet the prohibition rules, so the placard must match a real hazard of the load.
notes.evidence: Placards may be displayed for a hazardous material, even when not required, if the placarding otherwise conforms to the requirements of this subpart.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.502(c), PDF p. 284

notes.front: Where must a placarded transport vehicle, freight container or bulk packaging display its placards?
notes.back: On each side and each end.
notes.explanation: That is four placards on a box van or tank: one on each side and one at each end.
notes.evidence: must be placarded on each side and each end with the type of placards specified in tables 1 and 2 of this section
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.504(a), PDF p. 284

notes.front: When may a DANGEROUS placard be used instead of separate placards?
notes.back: When non-bulk packages of two or more Table 2 categories that need different placards are in one freight container, transport vehicle or rail car.
notes.explanation: It is an option (“may”), and it replaces only the Table 2 placards, not Table 1 placards.
notes.evidence: contains nonbulk packages with two or more categories of hazardous materials that require different placards specified in table 2 of paragraph (e) of this section may be placarded with a DANGEROUS placard
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.504(b), PDF p. 284

notes.front: When must a load placarded DANGEROUS also carry a category’s own Table 2 placard?
notes.back: When 1,000 kg (2,205 pounds) aggregate gross weight or more of that category is loaded at one loading facility.
notes.explanation: The limit counts what is loaded at one facility, so a large consignment of one category is shown by its own placard.
notes.evidence: However, when 1,000 kg (2,205 pounds) aggregate gross weight or more of one category of material is loaded therein at one loading facility
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.504(b), PDF p. 284

notes.front: A trailer is loaded at one facility with 1,200 kg of Class 3 drums and 300 kg of Class 8 boxes, all non-bulk. Which placarding meets § 172.504?
notes.back: B: FLAMMABLE placards for the Class 3, whichever way the Class 8 is placarded.
notes.choices:
A) DANGEROUS placards alone, because the load is mixed
B) FLAMMABLE placards for the Class 3, whichever way the Class 8 is placarded
C) No placards, because each category is under 454 kg
D) CORROSIVE placards only, because Class 8 is listed later in Table 2
notes.choicesExplained: A: the Class 3 reaches 1,000 kg at one facility, so its own placard is required. C: the exception looks at the aggregate of all Table 2 material (1,500 kg here), and the Class 3 alone exceeds 454 kg. D: nothing in § 172.504 favours a later-listed class; the Class 3 needs its placard.
notes.explanation: The 1,000 kg limit applies category by category: the Class 3 reaches it, so its own placard must be applied.
notes.evidence: the placard specified in table 2 of paragraph (e) of this section for that category must be applied.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.504(b), PDF p. 284

notes.front: Can a DANGEROUS placard replace a Table 1 placard, such as EXPLOSIVES 1.1?
notes.back: No. The DANGEROUS option in § 172.504(b) covers only materials that need Table 2 placards.
notes.explanation: Table 1 placards are always shown for their material; only Table 2 placards can be merged into DANGEROUS.
notes.evidence: may be placarded with a DANGEROUS placard instead of the separate placarding specified for each of the materials in table 2 of paragraph (e) of this section.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.504(b), PDF p. 284

notes.front: By highway or rail, when are placards not required for Table 2 materials in a transport vehicle or freight container?
notes.back: When it contains less than 454 kg (1,001 pounds) aggregate gross weight of Table 2 materials.
notes.explanation: The test is the aggregate gross weight of all Table 2 material aboard, not the weight of any one package.
notes.evidence: A transport vehicle or freight container which contains less than 454 kg (1001 pounds) aggregate gross weight of hazardous materials covered by table 2
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.504(c)(1), PDF p. 284

notes.front: Which two things are excluded from the under-454 kg placarding exception?
notes.back: Bulk packagings, and hazardous materials subject to § 172.505 (subsidiary-hazard placarding).
notes.explanation: Those loads must be placarded even if light; the exception is only for small non-bulk Table 2 loads.
notes.evidence: Except for bulk packagings and hazardous materials subject to § 172.505, when hazardous materials covered by table 2 of this section are transported by highway or rail
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.504(c), PDF p. 284

notes.front: If a vehicle falls under the 454 kg exception, may it still display placards?
notes.back: Yes, in the manner subpart F prescribes, unless § 172.502 otherwise prohibits it.
notes.explanation: The exception removes the duty, not the permission; the placards must still be correct for the load.
notes.evidence: The exceptions provided in paragraph (c) of this section do not prohibit the display of placards in the manner prescribed in this subpart, if not otherwise prohibited (see § 172.502)
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.504(c), PDF p. 285

notes.front: A box truck carries 400 kg aggregate gross weight of Class 8 in non-bulk drums and nothing else hazardous. What placards does the highway trip need?
notes.back: B: none are required, though CORROSIVE placards may be shown.
notes.choices:
A) CORROSIVE placards on each side and each end
B) None are required, though CORROSIVE placards may be displayed
C) One CORROSIVE placard at the front only
D) A DANGEROUS placard
notes.choicesExplained: A: the load is under 454 kg of Table 2 material, so placards are not required. C: placards, when used, go on each side and each end, never one alone. D: DANGEROUS is for two or more Table 2 categories, and nothing is required here anyway.
notes.explanation: Class 8 is a Table 2 material and the total is under 454 kg, so the exception applies; permissive placarding stays allowed.
notes.evidence: placards are not required on— (1) A transport vehicle or freight container which contains less than 454 kg (1001 pounds) aggregate gross weight
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.504(c), PDF p. 284

notes.front: A van carries a single 20 kg package of a Division 4.3 material by highway. Does it need placards?
notes.back: A: yes, DANGEROUS WHEN WET placards, because Division 4.3 is in Table 1.
notes.choices:
A) Yes, DANGEROUS WHEN WET placards on each side and each end
B) No, because a single package is never placarded
C) Only a DANGEROUS placard
D) No, because the load is under 454 kg
notes.choicesExplained: B: § 172.504(a) applies to any quantity; there is no single-package exception. C: DANGEROUS can replace only Table 2 placards. D: the 454 kg exception covers only Table 2 materials.
notes.explanation: The under-454 kg exception is written only for Table 2 materials, so a Table 1 material is placarded in any quantity.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.504(c) and (e), Table 1, PDF p. 285

notes.front: A cargo tank holds a small amount of a Class 3 liquid, under 454 kg in total. Must it be placarded?
notes.back: A: yes. The under-454 kg exception does not apply to bulk packagings.
notes.choices:
A) Yes, because the exception does not cover bulk packagings
B) No, because Class 3 is a Table 2 material under 454 kg
C) No, because a cargo tank is marked, not placarded
D) Only if it also carries a Table 1 material
notes.choicesExplained: B: Table 2 status does not help a bulk packaging, which is excluded from the exception. C: § 172.504(a) names bulk packagings among the things that are placarded. D: the Class 3 alone requires placards in bulk.
notes.explanation: The exception begins “Except for bulk packagings”, so a cargo tank is placarded whatever the quantity.
notes.evidence: Except for bulk packagings and hazardous materials subject to § 172.505
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.504(c), PDF p. 284

notes.front: Does a non-bulk packaging holding only the residue of a Table 2 material count when deciding on placards?
notes.back: No, unless the material is subject to § 172.505; such packaging need not be included.
notes.explanation: Residue-only non-bulk packages of Table 2 materials drop out of the placarding calculation.
notes.evidence: a non-bulk packaging that contains only the residue of a hazardous material covered by Table 2 of paragraph (e) of this section need not be included in determining placarding requirements.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.504(d), PDF p. 285

notes.front: A truck carries 300 kg of full Class 3 drums and 400 kg of empty Class 3 drums holding only residue. How many kilograms count towards the 454 kg test?
notes.back: C: 300 kg, because residue-only non-bulk packagings of Table 2 materials need not be included.
notes.choices:
A) 700 kg, because residue counts as full
B) 400 kg, because only the empties count
C) 300 kg, because residue-only non-bulk packagings need not be included
D) 0 kg, because Class 3 never needs placards
notes.choicesExplained: A: § 172.504(d) lets residue-only non-bulk packagings be left out. B: it is the empties that drop out, not the full drums. D: Class 3 is a Table 2 material with the FLAMMABLE placard.
notes.explanation: Leaving out the residue drums, the load is under 454 kg, so placards are not required by highway.
notes.evidence: need not be included in determining placarding requirements.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.504(d), PDF p. 285

notes.front: Which Table 1 placards go with Divisions 1.1, 1.2 and 1.3?
notes.back: EXPLOSIVES 1.1, EXPLOSIVES 1.2 and EXPLOSIVES 1.3 respectively.
notes.explanation: These three explosives divisions are in Table 1; the other three explosives divisions are in Table 2.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.504(e), Table 1, PDF p. 285

notes.front: Which Table 1 placard goes with Division 2.3?
notes.back: POISON GAS.
notes.explanation: Being in Table 1, it gets no weight allowance: any quantity is placarded.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.504(e), Table 1, PDF p. 285

notes.front: Which Division 5.2 material is in Table 1?
notes.back: Organic peroxide, Type B, liquid or solid, temperature controlled. It takes the ORGANIC PEROXIDE placard.
notes.explanation: Other organic peroxides are in Table 2 with the same placard, so only this group loses the weight allowance.
notes.evidence: 5.2 (Organic peroxide, Type B, liquid or solid, temperature controlled).
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.504(e), Table 1, PDF p. 285

notes.front: Which Division 6.1 material is in Table 1, and with which placard?
notes.back: Material poisonous by inhalation, with the POISON INHALATION HAZARD placard.
notes.explanation: This splits Division 6.1 across both tables; only the inhalation hazard loses the weight allowance.
notes.evidence: 6.1 (material poisonous by inhalation (see § 171.8 of this subchapter)).
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.504(e), Table 1, PDF p. 285

notes.front: Which Class 7 packages call for the RADIOACTIVE placard under Table 1?
notes.back: Packages bearing the Radioactive Yellow-III label.
notes.explanation: Table 1 limits the Class 7 row to the Yellow-III label; a footnote adds some further radioactive shipments.
notes.evidence: 7 (Radioactive Yellow III label only)
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.504(e), Table 1, PDF p. 285

notes.front: Which placard does Table 2 give Division 6.2 (infectious substances)?
notes.back: None.
notes.explanation: This matches § 172.500(b)(1), which takes infectious substances out of subpart F altogether.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.504(e), Table 2, PDF p. 285

notes.front: Which Table 2 placards go with Divisions 1.4, 1.5 and 1.6?
notes.back: EXPLOSIVES 1.4, EXPLOSIVES 1.5 and EXPLOSIVES 1.6 respectively.
notes.explanation: Only these three explosives divisions get the Table 2 weight allowance.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.504(e), Table 2, PDF p. 285

notes.front: Is Division 1.4 in Table 1 or Table 2?
notes.back: Table 2.
notes.explanation: Divisions 1.1 to 1.3 are in Table 1; Divisions 1.4 to 1.6 are in Table 2.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.504(e), Table 2, PDF p. 285

notes.front: Is Division 2.1 (flammable gas) in Table 1 or Table 2?
notes.back: Table 2, with the FLAMMABLE GAS placard.
notes.explanation: Of the gases, only Division 2.3 is in Table 1.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.504(e), Table 2, PDF p. 285

notes.front: Is a combustible liquid a Table 1 or Table 2 material?
notes.back: Table 2, with the COMBUSTIBLE placard.
notes.explanation: It has its own Table 2 row, separate from Class 3.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.504(e), Table 2, PDF p. 285

notes.front: What is the practical difference between Table 1 and Table 2 materials when loaded in non-bulk packages on a truck?
notes.back: Table 1 materials are placarded in any amount; Table 2 materials need placards only from 454 kg aggregate gross weight.
notes.explanation: The difference comes from paragraph (c), whose weight exception is limited to Table 2 materials moving by highway or rail.
notes.evidence: when hazardous materials covered by table 2 of this section are transported by highway or rail, placards are not required on
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.504(c), PDF p. 284

notes.front: If a load needs placards for more than one Class 1 division, which must be displayed?
notes.back: Only the placard for the lowest division number.
notes.explanation: For example, a load needing both EXPLOSIVES 1.1 and 1.4 placards displays only the 1.1 placard.
notes.evidence: When more than one division placard is required for Class 1 materials on a transport vehicle, rail car, freight container or unit load device, only the placard representing the lowest division number must be displayed.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.504(f)(1), PDF p. 285

notes.front: A truck carries enough Division 1.3 and Division 1.4 explosives to need both placards. Which EXPLOSIVES placard must it display?
notes.back: B: EXPLOSIVES 1.3 only.
notes.choices:
A) EXPLOSIVES 1.4 only
B) EXPLOSIVES 1.3 only
C) Both, side by side
D) A DANGEROUS placard
notes.choicesExplained: A: the rule picks the lowest division number, which is 1.3. C: only the lowest-division placard must be displayed. D: DANGEROUS cannot stand in for the Table 1 placard EXPLOSIVES 1.3.
notes.explanation: When more than one Class 1 division placard is required, only the lowest division number must be shown.
notes.evidence: only the placard representing the lowest division number must be displayed.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.504(f)(1), PDF p. 285

notes.front: On which packagings may a FLAMMABLE placard be used in place of a COMBUSTIBLE placard?
notes.back: A cargo tank or portable tank, and a compartmented tank car holding both flammable and combustible liquids.
notes.explanation: It is an option (“may”), so the COMBUSTIBLE placard remains correct on these packagings.
notes.evidence: A FLAMMABLE placard may be used in place of a COMBUSTIBLE placard on— (i) A cargo tank or portable tank.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.504(f)(2), PDF p. 285

notes.front: When is a NON-FLAMMABLE GAS placard not required on a vehicle carrying non-flammable gas?
notes.back: When the vehicle also carries flammable gas or oxygen and is placarded FLAMMABLE GAS or OXYGEN as required.
notes.explanation: The exception depends on the FLAMMABLE GAS or OXYGEN placards actually being displayed as required.
notes.evidence: placard is not required on a transport vehicle which contains non-flammable gas if the transport vehicle also contains flammable gas or oxygen
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.504(f)(3), PDF p. 285

notes.front: A truck is placarded FLAMMABLE GAS, as required, for its Division 2.1 cylinders, and also carries a Division 2.2 gas in placardable amounts. What must it show for the Division 2.2 gas?
notes.back: D: nothing more; the NON-FLAMMABLE GAS placard is not required alongside the FLAMMABLE GAS placards.
notes.choices:
A) NON-FLAMMABLE GAS placards on each side and each end
B) An OXYGEN placard as well
C) A DANGEROUS placard in place of both
D) Nothing more; the NON-FLAMMABLE GAS placard is not required
notes.choicesExplained: A: the exception in § 172.504(f)(3) removes this duty when FLAMMABLE GAS placards are displayed. B: an OXYGEN placard is for oxygen; nothing says the Division 2.2 gas is oxygen, and no further placard is needed. C: the rule already removes the second placard; DANGEROUS is an option for mixed Table 2 loads, not a requirement here.
notes.explanation: § 172.504(f)(3) drops the NON-FLAMMABLE GAS placard when the vehicle is already placarded FLAMMABLE GAS or OXYGEN as required.
notes.evidence: and it is placarded with FLAMMABLE GAS or OXYGEN placards, as required.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.504(f)(3), PDF p. 285

notes.front: When are OXIDIZER placards not required for Division 5.1 materials because of explosives in the same load?
notes.back: When the load also contains Division 1.1 or 1.2 materials and is placarded EXPLOSIVES 1.1 or 1.2 as required.
notes.explanation: A second paragraph gives the same relief with Division 1.5 and EXPLOSIVES 1.5 placards, for transport vehicles and rail cars.
notes.evidence: which also contain Division 1.1 or 1.2 materials and which are placarded with EXPLOSIVES 1.1 or 1.2 placards, as required.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.504(f)(4) and (5), PDF p. 286

notes.front: For domestic transport, which placard may replace the NON-FLAMMABLE GAS placard for compressed or refrigerated liquid oxygen?
notes.back: The OXYGEN placard (§ 172.530).
notes.explanation: The option is limited to domestic transportation and to these two forms of oxygen.
notes.evidence: For domestic transportation of oxygen, compressed or oxygen, refrigerated liquid, the OXYGEN placard in § 172.530 of this subpart may be used in place of a NON-FLAMMABLE GAS placard.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.504(f)(7), PDF p. 286

notes.front: When may the word OXYGEN be left off the OXYGEN placard?
notes.back: Only if the specific identification number is displayed on the placard.
notes.explanation: Hazard text is generally optional, but the OXYGEN placard must say what it is, by word or number.
notes.evidence: Text may be omitted from the OXYGEN placard only if the specific identification number is displayed on the placard.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.519(b)(3), PDF p. 290

notes.front: For domestic transport, when is a POISON INHALATION HAZARD placard not required?
notes.back: When the transport vehicle or freight container is already placarded with the POISON GAS placard.
notes.explanation: The exception is limited to domestic transportation.
notes.evidence: For domestic transportation, a POISON INHALATION HAZARD placard is not required on a transport vehicle or freight container that is already placarded with the POISON GAS placard.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.504(f)(8), PDF p. 286

notes.front: For domestic transport, when is a POISON placard not required?
notes.back: When the vehicle or freight container must display a POISON INHALATION HAZARD or POISON GAS placard.
notes.explanation: Like the POISON INHALATION HAZARD exception, it is limited to domestic transportation.
notes.evidence: For domestic transportation, a POISON placard is not required on a transport vehicle or freight container required to display a POISON INHALATION HAZARD or POISON GAS placard.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.504(f)(11), PDF p. 286

notes.front: How may a POISON placard be modified for Division 6.1 Packing Group III materials?
notes.back: It may display the text "PG III" below the mid line of the placard.
notes.explanation: It is an option (“may”); the text goes below the mid line of the placard.
notes.evidence: a POISON placard may be modified to display the text
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.504(f)(10), PDF p. 286

notes.front: Is a CLASS 9 placard required for domestic transport?
notes.back: No, including the part of an international journey within the United States. A bulk packaging must still display its identification number.
notes.explanation: The number may go on a CLASS 9 placard, an orange panel or a white square-on-point display.
notes.evidence: For Class 9, a CLASS 9 placard is not required for domestic transportation, including that portion of international transportation, defined in § 171.8 of this subchapter, which occurs within the United States.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.504(f)(9), PDF p. 286

notes.front: A cargo tank carries a Class 9 material on a domestic highway trip. What must it display?
notes.back: A: its identification number, on a CLASS 9 placard, an orange panel or a white square-on-point; the CLASS 9 placard itself is optional.
notes.choices:
A) Its identification number on a CLASS 9 placard, an orange panel or a white square-on-point
B) Nothing, because Class 9 is excepted domestically
C) CLASS 9 placards on each side and each end, without the number
D) A DANGEROUS placard
notes.choicesExplained: B: the exception is for the placard only; a bulk packaging still needs its identification number. C: the placard is not required, but the number is. D: DANGEROUS is for mixed non-bulk Table 2 loads, not a single bulk material.
notes.explanation: The domestic exception covers the placard, not the bulk identification number marking.
notes.evidence: However, a bulk packaging must be marked with the appropriate identification number on a CLASS 9 placard, an orange panel, or a white square-on-point display configuration
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.504(f)(9), PDF p. 286

notes.front: A material subject to the “Poison Inhalation Hazard” shipping description has a different primary hazard. What placards does its vehicle need?
notes.back: POISON INHALATION HAZARD or POISON GAS placards on each side and each end, in addition to any other placard for the material.
notes.explanation: The inhalation hazard is always shown, whatever the primary class; duplication of the placard is not required.
notes.evidence: must be placarded with a POISON INHALATION HAZARD or POISON GAS placard, as appropriate, on each side and each end, in addition to any other placard required for that material in § 172.504.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.505(a), PDF p. 286

notes.front: A tank holds a Class 8 liquid that is also poisonous by inhalation and described as such on the shipping paper. What placards are required?
notes.back: C: CORROSIVE placards plus POISON INHALATION HAZARD placards, on each side and each end.
notes.choices:
A) CORROSIVE placards only, because the primary hazard is Class 8
B) POISON INHALATION HAZARD placards only
C) CORROSIVE and POISON INHALATION HAZARD placards on each side and each end
D) A DANGEROUS placard
notes.choicesExplained: A: § 172.505(a) requires the inhalation-hazard placard in addition. B: the primary-hazard placard from § 172.504 is still required. D: DANGEROUS cannot stand in for these; it covers only mixed non-bulk Table 2 loads.
notes.explanation: § 172.505(a) adds the inhalation-hazard placard to whatever § 172.504 requires for the primary hazard.
notes.evidence: in addition to any other placard required for that material in § 172.504. Duplication of the POISON INHALATION HAZARD or POISON GAS placard is not required.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.505(a), PDF p. 286

notes.front: What extra placards does a vehicle, portable tank or freight container need for 454 kg or more of uranium hexafluoride?
notes.back: A CORROSIVE placard and a POISON placard on each side and each end, besides any RADIOACTIVE placard required.
notes.explanation: These subsidiary placards apply to non-fissile, fissile-excepted and fissile uranium hexafluoride alike.
notes.evidence: contains 454 kg (1,001 pounds) or more gross weight of non-fissile, fissile-excepted, or fissile uranium hexafluoride must be placarded with a CORROSIVE placard and a POISON placard on each side and each end.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.505(b), PDF p. 287

notes.front: What must a vehicle show for a material whose subsidiary hazard is being dangerous when wet?
notes.back: DANGEROUS WHEN WET placards on each side and each end, in addition to the placards § 172.504 requires.
notes.explanation: The water-reactive hazard is always placarded, even when it is not the primary hazard.
notes.evidence: has a subsidiary hazard of being dangerous when wet, as defined in § 173.124 of this subchapter, shall be placarded with DANGEROUS WHEN WET placards, on each side and each end
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.505(c), PDF p. 287

notes.front: Where must the hazard class or division number appear on a primary or subsidiary placard?
notes.back: In the lower corner of the placard.
notes.explanation: The rule applies the same way to primary and subsidiary placards.
notes.evidence: the hazard class or division number must be displayed in the lower
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.519(b)(4), PDF p. 290

notes.front: Who must provide placards to a motor carrier for a highway shipment, and when?
notes.back: The person offering the hazardous material, before or at the same time as offering it, unless the vehicle is already correctly placarded.
notes.explanation: The carrier then has its own duty: it may not transport the load until the placards are affixed.
notes.evidence: Each person offering a motor carrier a hazardous material for transportation by highway shall provide to the motor carrier the required placards for the material being offered prior to or at the same time the material is offered for transportation
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.506(a), PDF p. 287

notes.front: May a motor carrier transport a hazardous material in a motor vehicle whose required placards are not affixed?
notes.back: No. The required placards must be affixed before the carrier transports the material.
notes.explanation: The shipper supplies the placards, but the carrier may not move the load until they are on the vehicle.
notes.evidence: No motor carrier may transport a hazardous material in a motor vehicle, unless the placards required for the hazardous material are affixed thereto as required by this subpart.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.506(a)(1), PDF p. 287

notes.front: A shipper hands a driver 600 kg of Class 3 drums for a truck with no placards and says the driver should find some. The driver sets off unplacarded. Who has breached § 172.506?
notes.back: A: both: the shipper must provide the placards, and the carrier may not move the load until they are affixed.
notes.choices:
A) Both: the shipper must provide placards, and the carrier may not transport without them
B) Only the driver, because placards are the carrier’s job
C) Nobody, because 600 kg of Class 3 needs no placards
D) Only the shipper, and the driver may leave while waiting
notes.choicesExplained: B: § 172.506(a) makes providing the placards the offeror’s duty. C: 600 kg exceeds the 454 kg Table 2 allowance, so FLAMMABLE placards are needed. D: the carrier may not transport until the placards are affixed.
notes.explanation: § 172.506 puts a duty on each: the offeror provides the placards, and the motor carrier may not transport without them.
notes.evidence: shall provide to the motor carrier the required placards for the material being offered prior to or at the same time the material is offered for transportation, unless the carrier’s motor vehicle is already placarded
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.506(a), PDF p. 287

notes.front: Which freight containers must the offeror and the loading carrier placard under § 172.512(a)?
notes.back: Those with a capacity of 640 cubic feet or more.
notes.explanation: The 454 kg exception still applies to motor vehicles carrying such containers.
notes.evidence: a hazardous material in a freight container or aircraft unit load device having a capacity of 640 cubic feet or more shall affix to the freight container or aircraft unit load device the placards specified
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.512(a), PDF p. 288

notes.front: Outside air transport, what applies to a freight container under 640 cubic feet that is not placarded?
notes.back: It need not be placarded, but if not placarded it must be labelled under subpart E.
notes.explanation: Small containers can carry hazard labels instead of placards when no air leg is involved.
notes.evidence: in a freight container having a capacity of less than 640 cubic feet the freight container need not be placarded. However, if not placarded, it must be labeled in accordance with subpart E of this part.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.512(b)(2), PDF p. 288

notes.front: Who affixes placards to a bulk packaging containing a hazardous material?
notes.back: The person who offers the bulk packaging for transportation.
notes.explanation: For bulk packagings the offeror affixes the placards named in §§ 172.504 and 172.505.
notes.evidence: each person who offers for transportation a bulk packaging which contains a hazardous material, shall affix the placards specified for the material in §§ 172.504 and 172.505.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.514(a), PDF p. 288

notes.front: Must an emptied bulk packaging that needed placards stay placarded?
notes.back: Yes, unless cleaned and purged, refilled so residue is not hazardous, holding Class 9 residue below the reportable quantity, or an empty intermediate bulk container.
notes.explanation: Each way out removes the residue's hazard or leaves residue too slight to matter; the empty intermediate bulk container exception, for containers moved under § 173.29(d), was added from 3 September 2026.
notes.evidence: Each bulk packaging that is required to be placarded when it contains a hazardous material, must remain placarded when it is emptied, unless it— (1) Is sufficiently cleaned of residue and purged of vapors to remove any potential hazard;
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.514(b), PDF p. 288

notes.front: A cargo tank has just unloaded its Class 3 cargo but has not been cleaned or purged. The driver wants to remove the FLAMMABLE placards for the empty return. May they?
notes.back: D: no; the tank must stay placarded until cleaned and purged, or refilled so any residue is no longer hazardous.
notes.choices:
A) Yes, because an empty tank carries no hazardous material
B) Yes, if the trip is under 454 kg
C) Yes, if the driver keeps the shipping paper
D) No, not until it is cleaned and purged or refilled so residue is no longer hazardous
notes.choicesExplained: A: § 172.514(b) treats the emptied tank as still needing placards. B: the 454 kg exception never applies to bulk packagings. C: keeping a shipping paper does not replace placards.
notes.explanation: Unloading alone does not remove the hazard of the residue, and § 172.514(b) keeps the placards on.
notes.evidence: must remain placarded when it is emptied, unless it
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.514(b), PDF p. 288

notes.front: From where must each placard on a motor vehicle be clearly visible?
notes.back: From the direction it faces, except from the direction of another vehicle or rail car to which it is coupled.
notes.explanation: Placards on freight containers or portable tanks carried on the vehicle can meet this requirement.
notes.evidence: Each placard on a motor vehicle and each placard on a rail car must be clearly visible from the direction it faces, except from the direction of another transport vehicle or rail car to which the motor vehicle or rail car is coupled.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.516(a), PDF p. 289

notes.front: Where may the front placard of a tractor-trailer combination go?
notes.back: On the front of the truck-tractor, instead of or as well as on the front of the cargo body.
notes.explanation: Either position, or both, meets the requirement to placard the front of the motor vehicle.
notes.evidence: The required placarding of the front of a motor vehicle may be on the front of a truck-tractor instead of or in addition to the placarding on the front of the cargo body
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.516(b), PDF p. 289

notes.front: What must a placard be located clear of, under § 172.516(c)(2)?
notes.back: Appurtenances and devices such as ladders, pipes, doors and tarpaulins.
notes.explanation: Anything fixed to or hanging over the vehicle can hide the placard, so it must be placed clear of them.
notes.evidence: Be located clear of appurtenances and devices such as ladders, pipes, doors, and tarpaulins;
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.516(c)(2), PDF p. 289

notes.front: How far from other markings, such as advertising, must a placard be?
notes.back: Far enough not to reduce its effectiveness substantially, and in any case at least 3 inches (76.0 mm).
notes.explanation: Advertising near a placard can reduce its effectiveness, so the rule sets a minimum gap.
notes.evidence: Be located away from any marking (such as advertising) that could substantially reduce its effectiveness, and in any case at least 3 inches (76.0 mm.) away from such marking;
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.516(c)(4), PDF p. 289

notes.front: Who must keep placards in legible condition during transport?
notes.back: The carrier, so that format, legibility, colour and visibility are not substantially reduced by damage, deterioration or dirt.
notes.explanation: Damage, deterioration and obscurement by dirt are the causes the rule names.
notes.evidence: Be maintained by the carrier in a condition so that the format, legibility, color, and visibility of the placard will not be substantially reduced due to damage, deterioration, or obscurement by dirt or other matter;
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.516(c)(6), PDF p. 289

notes.front: A tanker driver mounts the side placard directly behind a ladder, where the rungs cross it. Is that allowed?
notes.back: C: no; the placard must be clear of appurtenances such as ladders, pipes, doors and tarpaulins.
notes.choices:
A) Yes, if the placard is at least 250 mm on each side
B) Yes, because the ladder is part of the tank
C) No, the placard must be clear of ladders and similar appurtenances
D) Yes, if the other side of the tank has a clear placard
notes.choicesExplained: A: size does not cure an obscured placard. B: the rule names ladders among the appurtenances to keep clear of. D: each side and each end need their own visible placard.
notes.explanation: A placard partly hidden by a ladder cannot be clearly visible from the direction it faces.
notes.evidence: Be located clear of appurtenances and devices such as ladders, pipes, doors, and tarpaulins;
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.516(c)(2), PDF p. 289

notes.front: What is the minimum size of a diamond placard?
notes.back: At least 250 mm (9.84 inches) on each side, with a solid inner border about 12.5 mm inside the edge.
notes.explanation: The 12.5 mm is measured from the outside edge of the placard to the outside of the inner border line.
notes.evidence: Each diamond (square-onpoint) placard prescribed in this subpart must measure at least 250 mm (9.84 inches) on each side and must have a solid line inner border approximately 12.5 mm inside and parallel to the edge.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.519(c)(1), PDF p. 290

notes.front: May a placard made before 1 January 2017 to the earlier size rule still be used?
notes.back: Yes, for domestic transport, until the end of its useful life, if colour tolerances are maintained.
notes.explanation: The allowance is domestic only, and colour tolerances must still be maintained.
notes.evidence: For domestic transportation, a placard manufactured prior to January 1, 2017, in conformance with the requirements of this paragraph in effect on December 31, 2014, may continue in service until the end of its useful life
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.519(c)(1), PDF p. 290

notes.front: A shipper offers new placards measuring 200 mm on each side for a domestic truck load. Are they acceptable?
notes.back: B: no; placards must measure at least 250 mm on each side.
notes.choices:
A) Yes, for domestic transport
B) No, placards must be at least 250 mm on each side
C) Yes, if the colours are correct
D) Yes, if they are hinged
notes.choicesExplained: A: the domestic allowance is for placards made before 1 January 2017 to the earlier rule. C: correct colour does not make up for size. D: hinging is allowed but does not change the minimum size.
notes.explanation: The pre-2017 allowance covers only placards made before 1 January 2017 to the earlier rule, not new ones.
notes.evidence: must measure at least 250 mm (9.84 inches) on each side
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.519(c)(1), PDF p. 290

notes.front: How tall must the hazard class or division number on a placard be, unless subpart F says otherwise?
notes.back: At least 41 mm (1.6 inches). Hazard text, when displayed, must also be at least 41 mm.
notes.explanation: Some placards set their own figures, such as 64 mm for the division numeral on the EXPLOSIVES 1.4 to 1.6 placards.
notes.evidence: the hazard class or division number, as appropriate, must be shown in numerals measuring at least 41 mm (1.6 inches) in height.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.519(c)(2), PDF p. 290

notes.front: Is hazard text, such as the word FLAMMABLE, required on a placard?
notes.back: No, except on Class 7 placards and the DANGEROUS placard; the OXYGEN placard may drop its text only if it shows the identification number.
notes.explanation: The colour, symbol and class number carry the message; text is required only where § 172.519(b)(3) says so.
notes.evidence: For other than Class 7 or the DANGEROUS placard, text indicating a hazard (for example, ‘‘FLAMMABLE’’) is not required.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.519(b)(3), PDF p. 290

notes.front: When international placards may be used under subpart C of part 171, which loads must still be placarded under subpart F?
notes.back: A bulk packaging, transport vehicle or freight container containing a material poisonous by inhalation.
notes.explanation: The international alternatives cover most placards, but not those for material poisonous by inhalation.
notes.evidence: However, a bulk packaging, transport vehicle, or freight container containing a material poisonous by inhalation (see § 171.8 of this subchapter) must be placarded in accordance with this subpart
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.519(f), PDF p. 291

notes.front: What does the EXPLOSIVES 1.4 placard look like?
notes.back: Orange, with the division numeral 1.4 at least 64 mm high, and black text, numerals and inner border.
notes.explanation: The asterisk is replaced with the compatibility group letter when required.
notes.evidence: The division numeral, 1.4, must measure at least 64 mm (2.5 inches) in height. The text, numerals and inner border must be black.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.523, PDF p. 292

notes.front: When may the word GASOLINE replace the word FLAMMABLE on a placard?
notes.back: On a cargo tank or portable tank being used to transport gasoline by highway.
notes.explanation: The word must be shown in white.
notes.evidence: The word ‘‘GASOLINE’’ may be used in place of the word ‘‘FLAMMABLE’’ on a placard that is displayed on a cargo tank or a portable tank being used to transport gasoline by highway. The word ‘‘GASOLINE’’ must be shown in white.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.542(c), PDF p. 295

notes.front: How do the FLAMMABLE and COMBUSTIBLE placards differ in use?
notes.back: FLAMMABLE is for Class 3 flammable liquids; COMBUSTIBLE is for combustible liquids, and is never needed for them in non-bulk packagings.
notes.explanation: Both are red; the difference is the material and the non-bulk exclusion for combustible liquids in § 172.500(b)(5).
notes.evidence: Combustible liquids in non-bulk packagings.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.500(b)(5) and § 172.504(e), PDF p. 284

notes.front: A placard has a white lower portion and a yellow triangle in its upper portion. Which placard is it?
notes.back: The RADIOACTIVE placard.
notes.explanation: The CORROSIVE placard reverses the idea: black below, with a white triangle above.
notes.evidence: the background color on the RADIOACTIVE placard must be white in the lower portion with a yellow triangle in the upper portion.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.556(b), PDF p. 299

notes.front: A placard is blue with white symbol, text and class number. Which placard is it, and which table lists it?
notes.back: The DANGEROUS WHEN WET placard, in Table 1.
notes.explanation: No other placard in subpart F has a blue background.
notes.evidence: the background color on the DANGEROUS WHEN WET placard must be blue.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.548(b), PDF p. 296

notes.front: Two placards have an all-yellow background with black symbol and text. Which are they?
notes.back: The OXYGEN placard (class number 2) and the OXIDIZER placard (division number 5.1).
notes.explanation: They share colour and symbol; the number in the lower corner tells them apart.
notes.evidence: the background color on the OXIDIZER placard must be yellow. The symbol, text, division number and inner border must be black.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), §§ 172.530 and 172.550, PDF p. 296

notes.front: Two placards share a white field with a black upper diamond around the symbol. Which are they, and how do you tell them apart?
notes.back: POISON GAS and POISON INHALATION HAZARD; the class number (2 or 6) in the lower corner tells them apart.
notes.explanation: Both colour schemes are set in identical words in §§ 172.540 and 172.555.
notes.evidence: the background on the POISON INHALATION HAZARD placard and the symbol must be white.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), §§ 172.540 and 172.555, PDF p. 298

notes.front: A white placard with a black skull and crossbones shows the word “Toxic”. Is that allowed on a POISON placard?
notes.back: Yes. The word “Toxic” may be used instead of “Poison” on the POISON placard.
notes.explanation: § 172.554 allows the alternative word; the white background and black symbol stay the same.
notes.evidence: The word ‘‘TOXIC’’ may be used in lieu of the word ‘‘POISON’’.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.554(b), PDF p. 298
